header.question:
A document in the library contains this sentence:

> Using individual neurons as these units has had some success (Olah et al., 2020; Bills et al., 2023), but a key challenge has been that neurons are often polysemantic, activating for several unrelated types of feature (Olah et al., 2020).

Check what the sentence says about the work it cites against that work in the library. Does the cited source support it? Cite the page(s) of the cited source that show what it actually says.

args.text:
Verdict: supported

The sentence comes from *Sparse Autoencoders Find Highly Interpretable Features in Language Models* (arxiv:2309.08600/v3/p1). It cites Olah et al., 2020, which is *Zoom In: An Introduction to Circuits* in the library, and Bills et al., 2023, *Language models can explain neurons in language models*, which appears only as an entry in the citing paper's reference list (arxiv:2309.08600/v3/p10) and is not itself in the library.

"Neurons as units have had some success": Zoom In says "thousands of hours of studying individual neurons have led us to believe the typical case is that neurons (or in some cases, other directions in the vector space of neuron activations) are understandable" (distill:zoom-in/r1/b22).

"Neurons are often polysemantic, activating for several unrelated types of feature": Zoom In says "Neural networks often contain “polysemantic neurons” that respond to multiple unrelated inputs. For example, InceptionV1 contains one neuron that responds to cat faces, fronts of cars, and cat legs." (distill:zoom-in/r1/b62). It also says this neuron is "not some subtle shared feature" (distill:zoom-in/r1/b64).

"A key challenge": Zoom In says "polysemantic neurons are a major challenge for the circuits agenda, significantly limiting our ability to reason about neural networks" (distill:zoom-in/r1/b65).

events.delta:
Verdict: supported

The sentence is from *Sparse Autoencoders Find Highly Interpretable Features in Language Models* (arxiv:2309.08600/v3/p1). It cites two works:

- **Olah et al., 2020** is *Zoom In: An Introduction to Circuits*, and the library has the full text.
- **Bills et al., 2023** is *Language models can explain neurons in language models*. The library doesn't have it. It only shows up in the citing paper's reference list (arxiv:2309.08600/v3/p10). So I could only check what the sentence attributes to Olah et al.

What Zoom In says on each point the sentence attributes to it:

- **Individual neurons have had some success as units.** Zoom In says "thousands of hours of studying individual neurons have led us to believe the typical case is that neurons (or in some cases, other directions in the vector space of neuron activations) are understandable" (distill:zoom-in/r1/b22).
- **Neurons are often polysemantic and respond to several unrelated features.** Zoom In says "Neural networks often contain “polysemantic neurons” that respond to multiple unrelated inputs. For example, InceptionV1 contains one neuron that responds to cat faces, fronts of cars, and cat legs." (distill:zoom-in/r1/b62). It adds that the neuron is responding to separate things, "not some subtle shared feature" (distill:zoom-in/r1/b64).
- **Polysemanticity is a key challenge.** Zoom In says "polysemantic neurons are a major challenge for the circuits agenda, significantly limiting our ability to reason about neural networks" (distill:zoom-in/r1/b65).

The sentence is a fair summary of Zoom In, and in places it uses nearly the same words ("often", "unrelated", "challenge"). It is a little milder than the source on one point: Zoom In claims that neurons are typically understandable, which is stronger than "some success". The neurons Zoom In studies are in an image model (InceptionV1), not a language model.
